findings.finding: Insights: For any n, a triple (1,a,n−a−1) works iff a|n−1, a≥2, a≠(n−1)/2. Thus f(n)=min_{a|n−1, a≥2, a≠(n−1)/2} (n−1−a) but also ≥⌈n/3⌉. For huge n≈M (odd), the smallest N comes from the largest proper divisor a of n−1 (≈n/2), giving f(n)≈(n−1)/2. Hence (2025!·f(M+c))/M≈(2025!/2)·(M+c)/M≈2025!/2 (since c≪M). Floor yields either ⌊2025!/2⌋ or ⌈2025!/2⌉ depending on parity of c. Compute g(c)=⌊2025!/2⌋/2025! or ⌈2025!/2⌉/2025!. Sum the six g’s, reduce to p/q, then output (p+q) mod 99991.

Insights: f(n) = min LCM of three distinct divisors summing to n. For n where n‑1 has a proper divisor ≥3, optimal triple is (1,d,m) with m=n‑1‑d, d|m, giving f(n)=m where d=(n‑1)/s, s = smallest divisor of n‑1 with 3≤s<n‑1. If n‑1 prime, need other construction. Use this to compute f(M+c) for huge M=3^{2025!} (M mod small numbers via fast exponent). Then g(c)=⌊2025!·f(M+c)/M⌋/2025! gives a rational with denominator 2025!. Sum the six g’s, reduce to p/q, output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfall: handle cases where n‑1 lacks proper divisor ≥3 (prime) and ensure distinctness (d>1). Use modular arithmetic for M and divisor search.

Insights: f(N)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=N. For N≈M (M=3^{2025!}), any triple must include M (else sum≤0.48M). So f(N)=M iff N−M can be written as sum of two distinct powers of 3 (<M). Otherwise f(N)>M. For tiny c (≤≈3·10⁸) this holds → g(c)=1. Need to test each given c, especially c=0,4M,1848374,… to decide if N−M is sum of two distinct powers of 3; for c=4M (N=5M) max may exceed M, requiring new analysis. Compute floor(2025!·f(N)/M) for each, sum, reduce p/q, find (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfall: ensure distinct powers, handle c=0 (requires three distinct divisors summing to M, not just M+0).

Insights: f(N)=min L s.t. N = d₁+d₂+d₃ with distinct divisors of L. Best ratio L/N =1/(1+1/x+1/y+1/z) (x,y,z|L). For huge N=M+small c, M=3^{2025!}≡1 (mod m) for any m coprime to 3. Check small divisor‑sets (2,3,6) → ratio 6/11 requires N≡0 (mod 11); not satisfied. Next best (2,4,8) → ratio 4/7 needs N≡0 (mod 7); not satisfied. Test all triples (x,y,z) with x<y<z≤30, compute ratio r= L/N = xyz/(xy+yz+zx+x+y+z). For each N (c=0,4M,1848374,…), find smallest L = ceil(r·N) that also admits a divisor‑set achieving N. Then g(c)=⌊2025!·L/M⌋/2025!. Sum six g(c)=p/q; output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure L’s divisors include the triple; handle N=5M (c=4M) where N≡5 (mod d) not 1. Use CRT for M mod d when d has factor 3. Use Python brute‑force over triples ≤30 (covers optimal ratios). Compute g(c) as integer/2025! and sum. Finally reduce fraction and mod.

Insights: f(n)=min c (largest of three distinct divisors) with a,b|c, a+b+c=n. For n≈M=3^{2025!}, optimal triple uses powers of 3, giving f(M)=2/3 M. In general f(M+δ)=⌊(2/3)(M+δ)⌋ or nearby values depending on δ’s representation as sum of two distinct powers of 3. Since 2025! contains all small factors, g(c)=⌊2025!·f(M+c)/M⌋/2025! equals the exact rational f(M+c)/M (denominator divides 2025!). Thus each g(c) is a simple fraction (e.g. 2/3, 1/2,…). Compute g for the six c’s, sum → p/q, reduce, then output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure f(M+c) uses the smallest c; handle cases where δ cannot be expressed as sum of two distinct powers of 3 (then f jumps to next feasible value). Use the smallest divisor s≥3 of (M+c−1) to get f via formula f=n−(n−1)/s when applicable.

Insights: f(n)=⌊6n/11⌋+d, where d depends only on n mod 11: d={0:0,1:2,2:1,3:1,4:2,5:2,6:1,7:1,8:2,9:2,10:1}. Write M=3^K, K=2025! (multiple of 11). For n=M+c, let B=⌊(6c+6)/11⌋+d((1+c)mod 11). Then f(M+c)=6·(M−1)/11+B. Hence g(c)=⌊K·f/M⌋/K=6/11+⌊K·B/M⌋/K. Since K≪M, ⌊K·B/M⌋=⌊K·(B/M)⌋, giving g(c)=6/11+⌊K·B/M⌋/K. Compute B for each c (using residues above), then g(c) as a fraction with denominator K. Sum six g’s → p/q; reduce; answer (p+q) mod 99991. (Key pitfall: ignore the tiny ε‑term; ensure K divisible by 11.)

Insights: For odd n, smallest n‑Norwegian N = (t‑1)(n‑1)/t where t = smallest divisor >2 of n‑1. Then  

g(c)=⌊2025!·(t‑1)(M+c‑1)/(t·M)⌋/2025! = ⌊K·(t‑1)·B/t⌋/K, with K=2025! and B=(M+c‑1)/M.  

For c≪M, B≈1 ⇒ g=1‑⌈K/t⌉/K (depends only on t).  

c=0,4M,265710644 ⇒ t=4 ⇒ g=3/4 (c=4M gives B≈5, so g=⌊K·3·5/4⌋/K=15/4).  

c=1848374 ⇒ t=11 ⇒ g=10/11.  

c=10162574 ⇒ t=5081287 (>K) ⇒ g=(K‑⌊K/t⌋‑1)/K.  

c=44636594 ⇒ t=17 ⇒ g=16/17.  

Sum these six fractions, reduce to p/q, compute (p+q) mod 99991 → 40958.

Insights: f(N)=min c> N/2 with two distinct proper divisors a,b of c, a+b=N−c. For huge M=3^{2025!}, N=M+tiny or 5M. c≈N/2; tiny offsets change c by O(1)≪M, so f(N)/M≈N/(2M). Hence g(c)=⌊2025!·N/(2M)⌋/2025!. Since 2025! is even, for N=M ⇒g=½; N=5M ⇒g=5/2; all other N give ½ (offsets ≪M). Sum=5=5/1 ⇒p+q=6 ⇒6 mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure ε=2025!·Δ/M<1 (Δ≤≈3·10⁸, M astronomically larger). Use parity of M (M≡1 mod 4) to confirm c₀ odd, so minimal c jumps to next even, but Δ stays O(1).

Insights: For any n, minimal X (f(n)) ≥ 6n/11 (use X plus its two largest proper divisors X/2,X/3). Equality holds when n≡0 (mod 11); otherwise f(n)=⌈6n/11⌉+O(1) (add ≤~200). Since M=3^{2025!}≫2025!·O(1), for n=M+c we have  

2025!·f(n)/M = 2025!·6/11 + ε, 0≤ε<1.  

Thus ⌊2025!·f(n)/M⌋ = 2025!·6/11 for all six c.  

So each g(c)=6/11, sum=36/11 ⇒ p+q=36+11=47.  

Pitfall: assume f≈n; actually f≈6n/11 with tiny additive error, making floor stable.

Insights: f(N)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=N ⇒ optimal triple has c=LCM and a,b are its two largest proper divisors. Then N=c(1+1/p+1/r) where p=smallest prime factor of c, r=p² or next factor q. So N must be divisible by D=p r+p+r (or p²+p+1). Ratio = pr/D (or p²/D). For each N, smallest ratio comes from smallest D dividing N. Compute for given N (M+c) using M≡1 (mod d) if 3∤d, else 0. Check divisibility by D∈{7,11,13,17,23,31,35,…}. Use floor((2025!·f(N))/M)=⌊2025!·ratio⌋. Sum six g(c), reduce to p/q, output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure D coprime to 3 (use M≡1), handle c=4M (N≡5 mod d). Use correct reduction of fractions.
